Swiss Electrical Equipment Sector Closes Strong Year with Steady Growth

The Swiss electrical equipment industry reported solid annual results this week, closing out 2023 with steady growth across key segments. According to figures released by the Swiss Electrical Manufacturers’ Association (SEMA), sector revenues rose 5.2% year-on-year to CHF 13.7 billion, buoyed by resilient domestic demand and ongoing investments in automation and energy efficiency.

Growth was broad-based, with the power transmission and distribution segment leading the way at 6.8%, followed by building automation and industrial controls at 5.1% and 4.6% respectively. Export activity remained a significant driver, with shipments to EU markets up 4.3% over the previous year. SEMA attributed the robust export performance to stable macroeconomic conditions in the euro area and continued demand for Swiss-made high-voltage components.

"Our members have demonstrated remarkable adaptability this year, responding to evolving customer needs in electrification and digitalization," said SEMA president Urs Huber at a press briefing in Zurich. "We saw particularly strong momentum in solutions for renewable energy integration and industrial automation."

Order intake for the fourth quarter was up 3.5% compared with Q4 2022, indicating ongoing healthy demand going into 2024. The association noted that supply chains had normalized after the disruptions seen in previous years, with most companies reporting lead times back to pre-pandemic levels.

Product innovation remained a focus for the sector, with several firms launching new offerings in smart grid technology and energy storage systems. "Swiss engineering continues to set benchmarks for reliability and innovation," said Andrea Lenz, Senior Analyst at Alpen Capital Markets. "The emphasis on R&D and investment in workforce skills has helped the industry maintain its competitive edge."

Employment in the sector was stable, with a slight increase of 1.2% in the total workforce, according to SEMA’s survey of its 42 member companies. Training programs and apprenticeships saw renewed interest, particularly in electrical engineering and automation technology.

Looking ahead, industry leaders expressed cautious optimism. "We expect the positive trend to continue, albeit at a more moderate pace," said Huber. "Energy transition initiatives across Europe and stable investment in infrastructure remain vital for our growth."

The Swiss electrical equipment industry, a key pillar of the country’s export-oriented manufacturing sector, continues to benefit from strong fundamentals and a reputation for quality and technical expertise.
